newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - CPI, manufacturing data due.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - CPI, manufacturing data due.

text.p: Investors have a plethora of U.S. data to deal with on Thursday, but the consumer price index (CPI) is likely to garner the most interest.

CPI was scheduled for release at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT along with initial weekly jobless claims. Shortly afterward, at 0915 EDT/1315 GMT industrial production and capacity utilization figures were due. Then at 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia's May regional survey and April real earnings were slated. CPI is seen rising by 0.1 percent and 0.2 percent excluding food and energy.

Economists surveyed by Reuters expected, on average, that industrial production would rise by 0.2 percent, down from March's 0.9 percent rise, and capacity utilization would come in at 84.1 percent -- flat, but still at a high level.

Traders took profits on Wednesday on the back of a weaker-than-expected reading on producer prices (PPI) as bond prices rallied. The weak reading fueled speculation that the Federal Reserve would be able to pause in tightening monetary policy when its policy-making arm meets next week.
Economists cautioned, however, that a weak PPI reading didn't necessarily bode for a similar CPI figure.
PPI fell 0.6 percent in April and 0.1 percent excluding the volatile food and energy components, versus consensus estimates of a flat overall reading.
"When you get these oddball moves in PPI, they're not usually replicated in CPI. It takes a lot more to tug CPI from its underlying trend," said Fred Sturm, economist at Fuji Securities Inc.

Sturm said bond market trading could be choppy as housing starts data is still had to be released on Friday after the CPI. Traders also had to contend with weekly unemployment claims, which the Fed was seen as closely eyeing.
Sturm said housing starts were habitually bad news for the bond market, with bond futures falling 75 percent of the time on days when they were released.
"We could end the week on a sour note. The market may just tread water," he said.
"A 25-basis-point rate hike by July 2 is all but a dead certainty, but I'm still flipping coins on whether they move May 20 -- right now it's about 51 percent to 49 percent," Sturm said.
"They don't have to hurry, there's nothing compelling them to move, he said.
"The market is probably susceptible to a further rise if CPI is as weak as some people see it being," said Michael McClure, head of government trading at Zions First National Bank.
For that to happen, a reading of no more than a 0.2 percent rise would be necessary in April consumer prices, he said.

McClure said talk of an impending budget agreement was having no effect on moving prices. Good news could move prices on the long bond back to the 97 level and yields to the low- to mid-6.80 percent levels, McClure said.
In late trading Wednesday the 30-year bond was up 16/32 at 96-23/24 to yield 6.88 percent.

At the short end the three-month bill was down four basis points at 5.03 percent. The six-month was off four basis points at 5.29 percent and the year bill was down three basis points at 5.52 percent.
Ten-year notes were up 8/32 at 99-19/32 to yield 6.68 percent. Five-year issues were up 5/32 at 100-12/32 to yield 6.53 percent and two-years were up 2/32 at 100-07/32 to yield 6.25 percent.
